title: The ball that waits for a lucky kick

data.source: Kramers (1940); Arrhenius (1889); Reiner (1964). Simulated first passages of the R4 rotor below its critical push, with thermal noise, seeded; exact first-passage integral by quadrature.

prediction: Below the critical push a cut is a thermal escape: waits follow Kramers and Arrhenius and are nearly memoryless (CV near 1) however the Deborah number changes; so the old dial "Omega ~ 1/De" with "CV = Omega/2" misses by more than a factor of 5 at every temperature, whichever way round it is read.
baseline: Kramers' escape rate (1940) and the Arrhenius law (1889).
why: With no noise the rotor rested and made no cut, in line with Phoenix's erratum. With noise the waits followed the exact first-passage integral and the Arrhenius slope, and their spread stayed near 1 while the Deborah number changed many-fold. The old dial predicted a spread that is hundreds of times too large one way round and hundreds of times too small the other. Phoenix's concordance note already calls the Deborah number standard rheology and the universal dial retired; this check gives the size of the miss in one system. The future test Phoenix suggests (one that beats rheology) was not attempted.
